photo.description: This graph shows the buildup of excess heat (thermal energy) in the ocean, land, ice, and atmospheric components of the Earth system since year 1960. The energy change is evaluated as ZettaJoules (=1021 Joules). The heat propagation to greater ocean depths with time is evident. Dashed lines bracket the total uncertainty of the data from the four components. Red line compares the trend of CERES satellite-based observations of the energy flow imbalance at top of atmosphere (TOA). Credits: ver1: von Schuckmann, K.; Cheng, L.; Palmer, M. D.; Hansen

pages.text: Oceans cover seventy percent of the Earth and store vast amounts of energy. This stored energy is known as ocean heat content. It serves as an important indicator of global warming and helps scientists understand our changing climate and environmental stability over time.
Between 1971 and 2018, oceans took in over ninety percent of the extra energy from global warming. Human greenhouse gas emissions are the main reason for this change.

Scientists measure ocean temperatures at many different locations and depths. Since the year 2000, an expanding network of nearly four thousand robotic Argo floats has helped measure temperature anomalies and changes in ocean heat all around the world.

Changes in ocean temperature greatly affect ecosystems in oceans and on land. Warming water affects marine life and causes variations in sea level and sea ice. It also changes the intensity of the water cycle and the migration of marine species.

Between 1971 and 2018, a steady upward trend in ocean heat content accounted for over ninety percent of Earth's excess energy from global warming. Increased ocean heat in response to anthropogenic carbon dioxide emissions is essentially irreversible on human time scales.

Ocean heat content measures the energy absorbed and stored by the world's oceans. Because oceans cover seventy percent of the Earth and have a high heat capacity, they play a critical role in climate stability.

Since 1971, a steady upward trend in ocean heat has accounted for over ninety percent of Earth's excess energy from global warming. This trend is driven primarily by human-caused greenhouse gas emissions that trap planetary heat.

Researchers track these changes using temperature data gathered from research vessels, stations, and an expanding network of nearly four thousand robotic Argo floats deployed globally since 2000 to measure subsurface temperature anomalies and ocean heat content.
While the upper ocean has warmed significantly, heat has also begun to penetrate deeper regions. The Southern Ocean has taken up a disproportionately large amount of this excess heat.

Warming oceans drive sea level rise, coral bleaching, and the migration of marine species. Monitoring ocean heat content remains essential for accurate climate models and understanding long-term trends.

C1-C2.headline: The Dynamics of Ocean Heat Uptake

pages.text: Ocean heat content quantifies the thermodynamic potential energy stored within seawater basins. Because oceans possess a high heat capacity and cover seventy percent of the planetary surface, they absorb the vast majority of excess anthropogenic heat.

Observational data reveals a robust multi-decadal upward trajectory, with ocean heat uptake accounting for over ninety percent of Earth's net energy imbalance since 1971. This persistent warming is fundamentally driven by rising atmospheric greenhouse gases.

Historical assessments relied on research vessels and stations, whereas contemporary monitoring utilizes approximately four thousand robotic profiling floats deployed through the international Argo program to measure subsurface temperature anomalies and track regional variations in heat uptake.

Regional variations in heat uptake are pronounced. The extratropical Southern Ocean has absorbed a disproportionate share of thermal energy, contributing to regional sea ice reduction and influencing global overturning circulation.

The resulting thermal expansion drives ongoing sea level rise and triggers ecological disruptions such as coral bleaching. Due to the immense thermal inertia of the oceans, these increases remain virtually irreversible on human time scales.
